name: Iñupiaq
notes: Iñupiaq (Iñupiatun), Inuit language of northern Alaska. Latin orthography (Webster–Zibell, 1970s); the values above follow the North Slope dialect. Three vowel qualities /a i u/, each with a long counterpart written double (aa, ii, uu) and therefore derivable from the single-vowel mapping. ⟨g⟩ = /ɣ/ vs ⟨ġ⟩ = /ʁ/; ⟨ł⟩ = voiceless lateral /ɬ/; ⟨sr⟩ = /ʂ/. Seward Peninsula and Uummarmiutun dialects differ slightly and are not separately modelled. Glottolog: `ik`/`ipk` is the Inupiaq macrolanguage, so the code is the `inup1234` family node by necessity.

sources.author: Kaplan, Lawrence D.

sources.notes: §1.2 The standard orthography and Table 1 (pp. 20-22), read on the page image. The table sets the Barrow and Kobuk consonant phonemes against the standard spelling: p t k q with ⟨'⟩ for the glottal stop, ⟨ch⟩ (and ⟨t⟩ before i) for the palatal affricate, ⟨kh k⟩ for x and ⟨qh q h⟩ for χ by position, ⟨g⟩ = ɣ, ⟨ġ⟩ = ʁ and also the uvular nasal, ⟨ł⟩ = ɬ, ⟨ḷ⟩ = ʎ, ⟨ł̣⟩ = the voiceless palatal lateral, ⟨sr⟩ = the voiced retroflex fricative and ⟨r⟩ = the retroflex approximant. Against this map: ⟨sr⟩ is voiced ʐ there, not ʂ; ⟨r⟩ is a retroflex, not the alveolar ɹ; and the dotted ⟨ḷ̣⟩ key is given as ɬ where the source has the voiceless palatal lateral, ɬ belonging to plain ⟨ł⟩. The source also notes that ⟨kh qh⟩ and ⟨h⟩ spell one fricative each by environment, which the map does not condition. Recorded here, not changed.

ancestors.notes: Eskimo-Aleut — the classification node this language sits under.

location.notes: Glottolog's computed centroid for the Alaskan Inupiaq family — a summary of a whole clade's range, not a place anyone speaks.
